Case_Content:
Man, 64 years old, no significant medical history, presenting with a left colon tumor revealed by subocclusive syndrome.  Thoraco-abdominal CT scan shows a 6 cm colonic mass and two liver metastases in segments II and V measuring 2.2 and 3 cm. CEA: 120 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, MSS. No extra-hepatic disease.
MDT Discussion: Metastases considered primarily resectable, symptomatic colonic lesion is the priority.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront – Both the obstructing left‑colon primary and the two synchronous liver metastases (2.2 cm in segment II and 3 cm in segment V) appear amenable to curative resection. No extra‑hepatic disease is present, and the size and number of hepatic lesions are within conventional criteria for hepatic resection. The primary tumor is symptomatic (obstruction) and therefore requires immediate treatment; the liver lesions are small, peripheral, and can be removed with limited parenchymal sacrifice, making a simultaneous or staged approach feasible.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Urgent surgical control of the primary tumor: perform a left‑sided colectomy (segmental resection or left hemicolectomy) to relieve the obstructive syndrome.  
• In the same operative session (if intra‑operative assessment confirms adequate liver remnant) or within a short interval (≤ 4 weeks), proceed to hepatic metastasectomy:  
 – Segment II: wedge resection or non‑anatomic segmentectomy.  
 – Segment V: wedge resection or non‑anatomic segmentectomy.  
 – Aim to preserve ≥ 30 % functional liver volume (future liver remnant) and avoid major vascular or biliary reconstruction.  
• Post‑operative systemic therapy: administer peri‑operative (adjuvant) chemotherapy, preferably a 6‑month course of FOLFOX (or CAPOX) given the RAS‑wild‑type status; consider addition of anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) as part of the adjuvant regimen.  
• Surveillance: serial CEA measurements and cross‑sectional imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
• Quantitative future liver remnant (FLR) ratio – needed to confirm that the planned hepatic resections will leave an adequate functional liver volume.  
• Detailed hepatic vascular and biliary anatomy (presence of vascular contact/invasion, arterial anatomy, biliary involvement) – essential to rule out the need for complex reconstruction.  
• Liver‑specific imaging (gadolinium‑enhanced MRI) – would better delineate lesion borders, vascular relationships, and detect any additional occult metastases.  
• Status of any prior systemic therapy – to ensure that chemotherapy‑induced liver injury (e.g., steatohepatitis) is not present, which could affect postoperative liver function.  

These missing items should be obtained (e.g., liver MRI with volumetry) before finalizing the operative plan, but they do not preclude proceeding with curative‑intent surgery as outlined.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with two liver metastases (segments II and V, 2.2 cm and 3 cm), bilobar but peripheral, without radiologic evidence of extrahepatic disease. Both lesions appear technically amenable to limited parenchymal-sparing resections (wedge/segmentectomy) with preservation of adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number, small size, and favorable location of metastases, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Priority: management of the symptomatic primary tumor
• The subocclusive presentation makes the left colonic lesion the immediate priority.
• Perform an oncologic left colectomy first (or ileostomy) with lymphadenectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) to treat the obstruction risk and allow safe continuation of the oncologic strategy.
• Alternative : consider a temporary diversion before colectomy according to exact degree of subocclusion.

B. Early systemic therapy after recovery from colectomy
• After the emergent procedure, perform high-resolution liver MRI to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement, evaluate arterial anatomy. Precise anatomic mapping is required to avoid intra operative surprise 
• Given the high CEA level (120 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT
• Initiate peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI).
• Given the high CEA level (120 ng/mL), the situation suggests biologically active disease; short-course neoadjuvant therapy allows treatment of micrometastases and assessment of tumor biology.
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy depending on MDT decision and tolerance.

C. Liver surgery after restaging (liver-first not indicated here due to symptoms)
• After 2–3 months of chemotherapy, perform high-resolution liver MRI and CT restaging.
• If stability or response is observed, proceed to parenchymal-sparing liver resections: segment II wedge/segmentectomy and segment V wedge/segmentectomy guided by intra-operative ultrasound.
• Aim for R0 margins (>1mm) while preserving maximal liver parenchyma.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Post-hepatectomy therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including pre-operative cycles).
• Close postoperative surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months given the initially high tumor marker level.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact degree of subocclusion and whether an temporary diversion is required before colectomy.
B. Detailed liver MRI describing vascular and biliary relationships of both metastases to confirm feasibility of parenchymal-sparing resections.
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy.
D. Exact location of the left colon tumor (descending vs sigmoid) influencing surgical planning.
E. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA
F. Patient’s nutritional status and postoperative recovery capacity, relevant for timing of chemotherapy.
G. Perform liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 56 years old, incidental discovery of a right colon tumor during a workup for iron deficiency anemia. Thoraco-Abdominal CT scan shows an ileocecal mass and a single 2.5 cm metastasis in segment VI. CEA 35 ng/mL, KRAS mutation present. No other lesions on FDG-PET.
MDT Discussion: Single peripheral metastasis, situation suitable for combined surgical treatment.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront – The liver lesion is solitary, 2.5 cm, peripheral in segment VI with no reported vascular or biliary involvement, and there is no extra‑hepatic disease. A limited hepatic resection (segmentectomy or wedge) will preserve an adequate future liver remnant. The primary right‑colon tumor appears resectable (no obstruction, perforation or bleeding reported). Therefore both the colorectal primary and the liver metastasis can be removed in a single operative session without the need for down‑staging therapy.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Pre‑operative work‑up:  
   – Complete colonoscopic evaluation with biopsy to confirm histology and grade.  
   – Contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or CT with liver protocol) to verify vascular anatomy, confirm absence of vascular contact, and calculate the FLR ratio.  
   – Baseline laboratory panel, cardiopulmonary assessment, and CEA repeat.  

• Surgical plan (simultaneous resection):  
   1. Laparoscopic or open right hemicolectomy with adequate lymphadenectomy (D3) to remove the primary tumor.  
   2. Open or laparoscopic segment VI resection (anatomic segmentectomy or non‑anatomic wedge) with ≥1 cm margin, preserving hepatic inflow/outflow.  
   3. Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion location and exclude additional occult metastases.  

• Post‑operative oncologic management:  
   – Start adjuvant systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6 months of FOLFOX or CAPOX) given KRAS‑mutated stage IV disease.  
   – Consider adding bevacizumab if high‑risk features are present.  
   – Serial CEA monitoring and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 – Missing data (most crucial for confirming the plan)  
• Grade of differentiation of the primary colorectal tumor (prognostic and may influence adjuvant therapy).  
• Confirmation that the primary tumor has not already been resected (surgical sequencing).  
• Presence or absence of vascular contact/invasion of the liver metastasis and detailed arterial/portal anatomy.  
• Calculated future liver remnant (FLR) ratio to ensure hepatic functional safety.  
• Whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been administered (could affect timing of surgery).  
• Clinical symptoms of obstruction, perforation or active bleeding from the colon lesion.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient has a single 2.5 cm peripheral metastasis in segment VI, no radiologically evident extra hepatic disease, and the lesion is amenable to a non anatomic wedge resection with an expected R0 margin. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered to be potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI and contrast enhanced CT to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement, evaluate arterial anatomy. Precise anatomic mapping is required to avoid intra operative surprise.

B. Systemic therapy
• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) because the tumor is KRAS mutated (no anti EGFR benefit).
• Re stage after chemotherapy with high resolution liver MRI (and contrast-enhanced CT).

C. Surgical management
• If restaging confirms continued resectability, perform a simultaneous right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) + a segment VI wedge/segmentectomy aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. (Simultaneous resection for solitary peripheral metastases is safe and oncologically equivalent to staged procedures 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Alternative : consider two-stage surgical resection of primary and liver tumors / consider right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) + an image-guided ablation using high-energy radio waves to generate heat via a probe (if no biliary or large vessels proximity)

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including the pre operative cycles). 
• Monitor CEA and imaging at 3 month intervals. A level of 35 ng/mL is acceptable but warrants close surveillance

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy. 
B. Potential extension of primary tumor to adjacent organ (abdominal wall, ureter, small bowel)
C. Detailed vascular/biliary relationship of the liver lesion – essential to confirm that a non anatomic resection will achieve clear margins without compromising hepatic inflow/outflow.
G. Patient’s nutritional status and postoperative recovery capacity, relevant for timing of chemotherapy.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
These items should be obtained before finalizing the operative plan.

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, history of smoking, presenting with T3N1 upper rectal adenocarcinoma with a single 1.8 cm liver metastasis in segment III. Pelvic MRI: limited parietal invasion. CEA 45 ng/mL. RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Single resectable metastasis, possibility of coordinated surgical treatment after short-course radiotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The single 1.8 cm metastasis in segment III is anatomically resectable, but the primary upper‑rectal T3N1 tumor requires neoadjuvant short‑course radiotherapy before definitive surgery. In addition, essential staging information (thoraco‑abdominal CT, liver MRI, assessment of vascular involvement and future liver remnant) is missing, making definitive surgical planning contingent on completing these steps.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Complete staging work‑up: obtain thoraco‑abdominal CT and liver MRI to rule out extra‑hepatic disease, define vascular anatomy, and calculate FLR ratio.  
• Initiate short‑course radiotherapy for the rectal primary (5 × 5 Gy).  
• During the radiotherapy interval (or immediately after), start peri‑operative systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX ± anti‑EGFR agent given RAS‑wild type) to address microscopic disease and potentially down‑size the liver lesion if any unfavorable features are identified.  
• Re‑stage after radiotherapy (repeat pelvic MRI and liver imaging). If the liver lesion remains resectable and FLR is adequate, proceed with a combined (simultaneous) approach: low anterior resection (or appropriate sphincter‑preserving rectal surgery) together with a segment III anatomical resection or wedge resection of the metastasis.  
• If simultaneous surgery is deemed unsafe (e.g., poor performance status, borderline FLR), adopt a staged strategy: first complete rectal surgery (post‑radiotherapy), then perform liver resection 4–6 weeks later after recovery.  
• Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy for at least 6 months, tailored to pathology (node status, tumor grade) and patient tolerance.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
• Grade of differentiation of the primary tumor (prognostic impact).  
• Thoraco‑CT and abdomen‑CT results (to exclude pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal or bone metastases).  
• Liver MRI findings, especially arterial anatomy and any vascular contact/invasion of the segment III lesion.  
• Calculated future liver remnant (FLR) ratio.  
• Whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been administered.  
These items are essential to confirm resectability, plan the extent of liver surgery, and finalize the peri‑operative oncologic regimen.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with a single 1.8 cm liver metastasis located in segment III. The lesion seems technically amenable to a parenchymal-sparing resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for solitary, small metastases, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI and contrast enhanced CT to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement, evaluate arterial liver anatomy. 

B. Systemic therapy
• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab or cetuximab)
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy depending on MDT strategy.
• Re stage after chemotherapy with high resolution liver and rectum MRI (and contrast-enhanced CT) to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control for both

C. Management of the rectal primary (oncologic priority)
• Given the T3N1 upper rectal tumor with limited parietal invasion, long-course radiotherapy is appropriate to optimize local control and allow coordinated surgical planning.

D. Coordinated surgical strategy
• Initiate doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or CAPOX) during the waiting period following radiotherapy. This period treats potential micrometastatic disease and tests tumor biology.
• Consider image-guided ablation of the single segment III lesion using high-energy radio waves to generate heat via a probe (if no biliary or large vessels proximity)
• After restaging with high-resolution liver MRI and pelvic imaging,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : resection / ablation of the segment III metastasis with follow up of primary tumor
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : resection / ablation of the segment III metastasis followed with strict follow up of primary tumor
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : liver-first resection or ablation of the single segment III metastasis, then rectal resection after appropriate recovery, using a staged or synchronous strategy : oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles).
– Parenchymal-sparing segment III wedge/segmentectomy aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins.
Simultaneous resection for solitary peripheral metastases is safe and oncologically equivalent to staged procedures
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact distance of the rectal tumor from the anal verge, influencing the type of rectal resection and anastomotic risk.
B. Presence of potential extra-hepatic involvement on 18FDG PET-CT . Chest CT.
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
D. Detailed relationship of the liver lesion to segment III vascular structures on liver MRI.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 72 years old, discovery at abdominal CT scan of a transverse colon adenocarcinoma, CEA 410 ng/mL, three liver metastases (segments IV, V and VI) measuring 2 to 3 cm. Liver MRI: partial contact with the right portal branch without invasion. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Primarily resectable metastases, simple liver surgery possible.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The liver lesions are limited (3 lesions, 2‑3 cm, confined to segments IV, V, VI) with only partial contact to the right portal branch and no radiologic invasion, which would be compatible with curative hepatectomy. However, decisive information is missing: a thoraco‑CT scan has not been performed to exclude pulmonary metastases, and the future liver remnant (FLR) ratio has not been calculated. Both are essential to confirm that a safe, oncologically complete resection can be achieved. Therefore resection is possible only after these prerequisites are addressed.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Complete staging: obtain a thoraco‑CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out lung metastases; perform volumetric CT or MRI to calculate the FLR ratio; confirm arterial and biliary anatomy of the right liver.  
• If staging confirms absence of extra‑hepatic disease and an adequate FLR (≥30 % for a normal liver), proceed with neoadjuvant systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX ± bevacizumab, or FOLFOXIRI given the high CEA and KRAS mutation) for 2–3 months to assess tumor biology and potentially downsize lesions.  
• Re‑evaluate imaging after chemotherapy: confirm that liver lesions remain resectable, that the FLR remains adequate, and that no new extra‑hepatic sites have appeared.  
• Surgical plan (assuming favorable reassessment):  
   – Perform a simultaneous resection: right hemicolectomy (or extended transverse colectomy) for the primary tumor followed by parenchymal‑sparing liver surgery (segmentectomy of segment IV and wedge resections of segments V and VI) preserving a sufficient FLR.  
   – If FLR is borderline, consider pre‑operative portal vein embolization of the right portal branch to induce hypertrophy before liver resection.  
• Post‑operative management: resume adjuvant chemotherapy to complete a total of 6‑12 months of systemic therapy, monitor CEA serially, and schedule surveillance imaging.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
• Thoraco‑CT (or PET‑CT) results – essential to exclude pulmonary metastases.  
• FLR ratio (volumetric assessment) – required to ensure safe hepatic resection.  
• Status of the primary colorectal tumor (resected vs. pending) – determines need for staged versus simultaneous surgery.  
• Grade of differentiation of the primary tumor – influences prognostic assessment and adjuvant therapy decisions.  
• Presence of obstructive, perforation or bleeding symptoms – would mandate urgent primary tumor resection before systemic therapy.  

These missing items are the most critical to finalize the resectability decision and to tailor the optimal treatment sequence.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with three liver metastases located in segments IV, V, and VI (2–3 cm), confined to the right liver and central segments. MRI shows only partial contact with the right portal branch and no evidence of vascular invasion. These lesions appear technically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resections or anatomicalm resection while preserving adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number and size of metastases with preserved vascular structures, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative systemic therapy (strongly recommended)
• The very high CEA level (410 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation suggest biologically aggressive disease.
• Given the high CEA level (410 ng/mL), perform chest CT scan and high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to assess extra-hepatic disease
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control according to patient tolerance.
• This allows treatment of potential micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology before surgery.

B. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to reassess the relationship of the lesions to the right portal branch and confirm maintained resectability.
• Evaluate future liver remnant (FLR) if right hepatectomy of considered.

C. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing strategy)
• If stability or response is observed, perform combined parenchymal-sparing resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
– Segment IV wedge/segmentectomy.
– Segment V and VI wedge resections.
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Management of the primary tumor
• Transverse colectomy of extended right colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.
• Otherwise, a staged approach with colectomy first is acceptable.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months given the high CEA level (410 ng/mL).

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Presence of potential extra-hepatic involvement on 18FDG PET-CT and chest CT scan.
B. Detailed vascular mapping on MRI to confirm absence of true portal invasion.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) calculation in case of right hepatectomy.F. Circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI, essential for rectal surgical planning. 
D. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Man, 59 years old, T3N1 sigmoid colon tumor associated with four peripheral liver metastases (segments II, III, V, VIII) at the abdominal CT scan. Maximum size: 2.9 cm. CEA 200 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, HER2 negative.
MDT Discussion: Primarily resectable lesions, no vascular or extra-hepatic involvement.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: the liver lesions are peripheral, ≤3 cm, without vascular contact (PresenceOfVascularContactOrInvasion = False) and there is no documented extra‑hepatic disease (all Extrahepatic = False). However, decisive information is missing: (a) whether the sigmoid primary has already been resected (ColorectalPrimaryTumorPostResectionCharacterization = Missing) or if it requires urgent surgery for obstruction/perforation; (b) quantitative future liver remnant assessment (FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery = Missing); and (c) confirmation of absent pulmonary metastases (ThoracoCTScanPerformed = Missing). These gaps must be resolved before a definitive upfront liver‑first or simultaneous operation can be planned.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Complete staging: obtain a thoracic CT scan to rule out occult lung metastases and a liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast to delineate lesion anatomy, arterial supply, and biliary proximity (addresses Missing items in ImagingExams and ArterialAnatomy).  
- Calculate FLR using volumetric CT or MRI; if FLR < 30 % in a normal liver, plan portal vein embolization (PVE) to hypertrophy the remnant.  
- Determine status of the primary tumor:  
   • If the sigmoid lesion is asymptomatic and not yet resected, schedule a simultaneous laparoscopic sigmoid colectomy and parenchymal‑sparing liver resections (wedge or segmental) of segments II, III, V and VIII.  
   • If the primary is symptomatic (obstruction, perforation) or if simultaneous resection is deemed unsafe, perform colon resection first, recover, then proceed to liver surgery.  
- Given RAS wild‑type status, incorporate peri‑operative systemic therapy per EORTC 40983 (FOLFOX ± anti‑EGFR) either as neoadjuvant (if FLR is borderline) or adjuvant for 6 months after surgery.  
- Post‑operative surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3–6 months.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Confirmation of whether the sigmoid primary has already been resected or requires urgent surgery (ColorectalPrimaryTumorPostResectionCharacterization, PresenceOfSymptomsForObstruction/Perforation).  
- Thoraco‑CT results to definitively exclude pulmonary metastases (ThoracoCTScanPerformed).  
- Quantitative FLR ratio to ensure safe hepatic resection (FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery).  
- Liver MRI and arterial anatomy details to plan precise parenchymal‑sparing resections (Has liver MRI been performed?, ArterialAnatomy).  

These items must be obtained before proceeding to definitive surgical management.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with four peripheral liver metastases (segments II, III, V, and VIII), all smaller than 3 cm, without vascular involvement or extrahepatic disease. The distribution is bilobar but the lesions are technically amenable to multiple parenchymal-sparing resections while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number, small size, and peripheral location of metastases, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative systemic therapy (recommended)
• The elevated CEA level (200 ng/mL) and multiplicity of lesions suggest biologically active disease.
• Given the high CEA level (200 ng/mL), perform chest CT scan and high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to assess extra-hepatic disease
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI).
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy according to MDT decision.
• This period treats micrometastatic disease and evaluates tumor biology.

B. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and reassess lesion relationships.

C. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing strategy)
• If stability or response is observed, perform multiple wedge/segmental resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
– Segments II–III resections (left lateral section wedges).
– Segment V wedge resection.
– Segment VIII wedge resection.
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Management of the primary tumor
• If the sigmoid tumor has not yet been resected, a simultaneous sigmoid colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis can be considered, provided the patient’s condition allows combined surgery.
• Otherwise, a staged approach with colectomy first is acceptable.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Presence of potential extra-hepatic involvement on 18FDG PET-CT and chest CT scan.
B. Detailed liver MRI describing vascular and biliary relationships of each lesion.
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy.
F. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 63 years old, right-sided T4N2M1 colon cancer, two liver metastases in segments II and IVa (3 and 4 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. Liver MRI: middle hepatic vein preserved. CEA 95 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Technically resectable metastases, with priority given to controlling the primary tumor.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- The liver lesions are described as “technically resectable” (segments II and IVa, middle hepatic vein preserved) but the analysis lists FutureLiverRemnantFLRRatio: Missing and PresenceOfVascularContactOrInvasion: Missing, both of which are decisive for operative feasibility.  
- The primary colon tumor is T4N2 and has not been reported as already resected (Has the colorectal primary tumor been already resected? Missing); high‑risk primary disease usually warrants neoadjuvant systemic therapy before any liver surgery.  
- Because a specific prerequisite (assessment of FLR and possible portal vein embolization) or a missing decisive piece of information (FLR ratio) is identified, the case fits the “Potentially resectable” category.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) given KRAS mutation (anti‑EGFR agents not indicated) and high‑risk T4N2 primary; this will treat occult disease and may downsize liver mets.  
- After 2–3 months, repeat high‑quality liver MRI and volumetric CT to:  
   • Re‑assess lesion‑vessel relationships (confirm absence of vascular invasion).  
   • Calculate future liver remnant volume; if FLR <20‑30 % consider portal vein embolization of the right portal branches to hypertrophy the left lateral sector.  
- Once FLR is adequate and lesions remain resectable, proceed with a staged approach:  
   1. Perform right hemicolectomy (primary tumor resection) – priority per MDT.  
   2. Within 4–6 weeks, perform parenchymal‑sparing liver resection of segment II and IVa (segmentectomy or limited anatomical resection) preserving the middle hepatic vein.  
- If intra‑operative assessment confirms sufficient FLR and the patient’s physiologic reserve is robust, a simultaneous colon and liver resection could be considered, but only after confirming FLR adequacy.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy to complete a total of 6 months (or longer per response) should follow liver surgery.  
- Ongoing surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3–6 months.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio and volumetric assessment.  
- Exact relationship of the metastases to hepatic vessels and bile ducts (vascular/biliary involvement).  
- Status of the primary tumor (has it already been resected or is it causing obstruction/perforation).  
- Timing of liver metastases (synchronous vs metachronous) to guide sequencing.  
- Whether any systemic therapy has already been administered.  
These missing items are essential to finalize resectability and to choose between simultaneous versus staged surgery.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with two liver metastases located in segments II and IVa (3 and 4 cm), without evidence of extrahepatic disease. MRI confirms preservation of the middle hepatic vein and no major vascular invasion. Both lesions are technically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resections (in case of effective tumor shrinkage with neoadjuvant therapy) or left hepatectomy with preservation of the middle hepatic vein. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number and favorable anatomical location of metastases, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Priority: control of the primary tumor
• The elevated CEA level (95 ng/mL) and right-sided T4N2 colon cancer represents locally advanced disease and is the immediate oncologic priority.
• Given the high CEA level (95 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to assess extra-hepatic disease
• Assess potential extension of primary tumor to adjacent organ (abdominal wall, ureter, small bowel, duodenum)
• 3 options
-	Perform an oncologic right hemicolectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis, first to control the primary tumor and prevent local complications.
-	Perform an derivation ileostomy first to control the primary tumor and prevent local complications during chemotherapy.
-	Initiate peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab).

B. Early systemic therapy after recovery
• Initiate peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab).
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.

Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning: The three liver metastases are small (1‑2 cm) and located in segments VI‑VIII, which in a patient with a normal liver would generally allow a curative‑intent hepatic resection. However, the structured analysis lacks decisive information required to confirm surgical feasibility:  
- FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery is missing, preventing confirmation that the future liver remnant will be sufficient.

Because these specific data points are absent, the case must be classified as “Potentially resectable” pending acquisition of the missing information.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Short‑course pelvic radiotherapy (5 × 5 Gy) for the upper‑rectal T3N0 primary, as already planned by the MDT.  
2. Neoadjuvant systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6 cycles of FOLFOX ± anti‑EGFR antibody given RAS wild‑type) initiated after radiotherapy to:  
   - Treat micrometastatic disease,  
   - Potentially downsize the hepatic lesions, and  
   - Provide an early assessment of tumor biology (CEA trend, radiologic response).  
3. Restaging work‑up after chemotherapy:  
   - Contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with hepatobiliary phase to delineate lesion margins, vascular/biliary relationships, and to calculate FLR volume.  
   - Thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to reconfirm absence of extra‑hepatic disease, including brain imaging if clinically indicated.  
4. Multidisciplinary reassessment of resectability based on MRI‑derived FLR ratio and vascular anatomy.  
5. Surgical plan (if resectability confirmed):  
   - Option A – Simultaneous resection: Low anterior resection with total mesorectal excision plus right posterior segmentectomy (segments VI‑VIII) or limited anatomical resection preserving ≥20 % FLR.  
   - Option B – Staged approach (if FLR insufficient): First perform colorectal resection (or radiotherapy‑only strategy) followed by portal vein embolization to hypertrophy the future liver remnant, then delayed hepatic resection.  
6. Adjuvant therapy: Completion of postoperative systemic chemotherapy (total 12 cycles) and consideration of adjuvant targeted therapy per molecular profile.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery (future liver remnant volume) – essential to decide whether hepatic resection can be performed safely.  
- Detailed hepatic arterial, portal, and biliary anatomy plus presence of vascular or biliary invasion – required to plan the extent of liver resection and to avoid intra‑operative complications.  
- Confirmation of whether the primary tumor has already been resected or is still in situ – influences timing of colorectal surgery.  
- Grade of differentiation of the primary tumor – may affect aggressiveness of systemic therapy.  
- Status of systemic treatment already administered (if any) – determines how many additional chemotherapy cycles are needed before surgery.  
- Thoraco‑CT and brain imaging results – to definitively exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
Acquiring these pieces of information will allow conversion of the “Potentially resectable” classification to “Resectable upfront” or, if unfavorable, to “Not resectable.”

Case_Content:
Woman, 70 years old, history of hypertension, discovery of left colon cancer and a single 2.7 cm liver metastasis in segment IVb at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 40 ng/mL. BRAF wild-type, MSS.
MDT Discussion: Isolated metastasis, anatomically favorable for a single resection.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning: The liver lesion (single 2.7 cm metastasis in segment IVb) is anatomically amenable to a parenchymal‑sparing resection, and there is no radiologic evidence of extra‑hepatic disease. However, decisive information required for definitive surgical planning is missing:  
- Whether the left‑colon primary has already been resected (or if it is symptomatic and requires urgent resection).  
- Detailed hepatic vascular anatomy and assessment of possible portal or hepatic vein involvement, which would be provided by a liver MRI.  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) volume/ratio to confirm that a segment IVb resection will leave an adequate functional liver.  
Because these items must be clarified before a safe operation can be scheduled, the case is classified as “Potentially resectable.”  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Complete staging work‑up  
   - Perform a high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to delineate vascular anatomy, confirm absence of portal/hepatic vein invasion, and allow volumetric FLR calculation.  
   - Review colonoscopy and pathology to determine the grade of differentiation and assess for obstructive, perforation or bleeding symptoms.  
2. Address the primary tumor  
   - If the left‑colon cancer has not yet been resected and is symptomatic (obstruction/bleeding) → proceed with curative colon resection first.  
   - If the primary is asymptomatic and technically feasible → plan a simultaneous colon and liver resection (single‑stage) to minimize overall treatment time.  
3. Liver surgery  
   - Assuming FLR ≥ 20 % (normal liver) and no major vascular involvement on MRI, perform a segment IVb anatomical or non‑anatomical (parenchymal‑sparing) resection with negative margins (R0).  
   - Use intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion location and margins.  
4. Systemic therapy  
   - Given a solitary, small metastasis and favorable biology (BRAF‑wild type, MSS), peri‑operative chemotherapy is optional. If the primary tumor required resection first and the patient has high‑risk features (e.g., high CEA = 40 ng/mL, unknown grade), consider 3–4 cycles of FOLFOX/XELOX before liver surgery (neoadjuvant) or as adjuvant after both resections.  
5. Post‑operative surveillance  
   - Monitor CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.  
   - Imaging (CT or MRI) at 6 months and annually thereafter, or sooner if CEA rises.  

Step 3 – Missing data (most crucial for decision)  
- Status of the colorectal primary (resected or not, presence of obstructive/bleeding symptoms).  
- Grade of differentiation of the primary tumor.  
- Liver MRI findings: vascular contact/invasion, arterial anatomy, and volumetric FLR assessment.  
- Whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been administered.  
- Confirmation of portal vein patency and absence of portal thrombosis.  

These items must be obtained to move from “Potentially resectable” to a definitive “Resectable upfront” plan.

- FLR ratio compatibility with surgery.

- Status of the primary colorectal tumor (resected or not) and presence of obstructive/bleeding symptoms.

Category: Potentially resectable

- The status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not) is unknown (ColorectalPrimaryTumorPostResectionCharacterization – Missing).  

These missing data constitute prerequisite steps before surgery; therefore the case is classified as “Potentially resectable.”

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Complete staging:  
   • Perform a contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary metastases.  
   • Obtain a liver‑specific MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to delineate lesion margins, vascular and biliary anatomy, and to calculate FLR volume.  
2. Assess and treat the primary tumor:  
   • If the primary lesion has not yet been resected, schedule a curative left‑sided colectomy (segmental resection or left hemicolectomy) as the first operative step, unless obstructive or perforation symptoms dictate urgent surgery.  
3. Systemic therapy:  
   • Initiate neoadjuvant combination chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) given the high CEA (330 ng/mL) and KRAS‑mutated status (anti‑EGFR agents not indicated).

   • If FLR ≥30 % (or ≥40 % in a steatotic liver) and no extra‑hepatic disease, proceed to liver resection.  
   • Consider a staged approach: primary colon resection first, followed by hepatic resection after systemic therapy response.  
   • If FLR is insufficient, plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) before definitive hepatic resection.  
6. Post‑operative management:  
   • Continue adjuvant chemotherapy to complete a standard 6‑month regimen, tailoring to pathologic response and margin status.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Thoraco‑CT (or PET‑CT) results to exclude pulmonary metastases.  
- Liver MRI findings (vascular contact, biliary involvement, precise lesion size, FLR calculation).  
- Confirmation of whether the primary colon tumor has already been resected.  
- Information on any prior systemic chemotherapy (type, cycles, response).  
- Assessment of hepatic arterial anatomy and presence of portal vein thrombosis, which influence resection strategy.  

These items are essential to move from “Potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.

Man, 57 years old, right T4aN2M1 colon cancer, seven bilobar liver metastases, sizes 1 to 4 cm at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 520 ng/mL, KRAS mutated. Liver MRI: vascular contact with the right portal branch.
MDT Discussion: Metastases not resectable upfront, considered for conversion chemotherapy FOLFOX + bevacizumab.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Classification: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning:  
- The MDT explicitly stated that the liver metastases are “not resectable upfront” and that conversion chemotherapy is planned.  
- Bilobar distribution with seven lesions (NumberOfMetastases: 7) ranging 1‑4 cm, and documented vascular contact with the right portal branch (PresenceOfVascularContactOrInvasion: True) make immediate anatomic resection unsafe.  
- No systemic therapy has yet been given (Has a systemic treatment already been performed? False), therefore a prerequisite down‑staging regimen is required before a surgical attempt can be considered.  
- Because a specific prerequisite (conversion chemotherapy) is identified, the case fits the “Potentially resectable” category rather than “Resectable upfront” or “Not resectable.”  

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Initiate conversion systemic therapy: FOLFOX + bevacizumab (KRAS mutated, thus anti‑EGFR agents are contraindicated).  
2. Re‑stage after 2–3 months (or after 4–6 cycles) with repeat liver MRI and thoraco‑abdominal CT to assess:  
   - Tumor response (size reduction, loss of vascular contact)  
   - FLR adequacy (FutureLiverRemnantFLRRatio)  
   - Any new extra‑hepatic disease (especially brain, which remains unevaluated).  
3. If imaging shows sufficient down‑staging and FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % in a steatotic liver), proceed to liver‑first approach:  
   a. If FLR is borderline, perform portal vein embolization of the future remnant.  
   b. Plan a curative‑intent hepatectomy (e.g., right trisectionectomy ± left lateral segment) respecting vascular and biliary anatomy; intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm margins.  
4. Address the primary colon tumor:  
   - If the primary remains unresected and is asymptomatic, consider simultaneous colon resection during the liver operation only if operative time and physiologic reserve allow (patient age 57, no reported comorbidities).  
   - If the primary is symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding) or if operative risk is high, resect the colon first (right hemicolectomy) followed by liver surgery after recovery.  
5. Post‑operative management:  
   - Continue adjuvant chemotherapy (e.g., additional FOLFOX cycles) for at least 6 months total.  
   - Monitor CEA (baseline 520 ng/mL) and imaging every 3–4 months for recurrence.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Grade of differentiation of the primary tumor (GradeOfDifferentation) – impacts overall prognosis and may influence aggressiveness of systemic therapy.  
- Status of primary tumor resection (Has the colorectal primary tumor been already resected?) – determines need for immediate colon surgery versus liver‑first strategy.  
- Presence of obstructive, perforative, or bleeding symptoms (PresenceOfSymptomsForObstruction/Perforation/Bleeding) – would mandate urgent primary tumor resection.  
- Exact hepatic segments involved (HepaticSegmentsInvolved) and arterial anatomy (ArterialAnatomy) – essential for planning the extent of hepatectomy and vascular control.  
- Future liver remnant ratio (FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery) – decisive for safety of major liver resection and need for portal vein embolization.  
- Evaluation of extra‑hepatic brain involvement (Missing) – must be ruled out before committing to curative surgery.  

These missing items are the most critical to finalize operative planning and to confirm that a curative‑intent liver resection will be feasible after conversion therapy.

Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has four bilobar liver metastases, one abutting the right hepatic vein, and no prior systemic therapy.    • Re‑assess vascular contact (right hepatic vein) and arterial anatomy,  
   • Calculate future liver remnant (FLR) volume and ratio.

The structured analysis lacks critical data that directly determine surgical feasibility: hepatic segment distribution, presence of vascular/biliary invasion, and the future liver remnant (FLR) ratio. Moreover, it is unknown whether the primary colon tumor has already been resected and whether any systemic chemotherapy has been administered. Because these missing pieces are decisive for planning a safe hepatectomy, resection cannot be performed upfront and requires further assessment and likely down‑staging therapy.

- Verify and, if needed, resect the primary left‑sided colon cancer first (either as a separate operation or simultaneous with liver surgery if intra‑operative assessment permits).

   • Stage 2 – completion hepatectomy of the remaining metastases, aiming for R0 resection. Consider ALPPS only if FLR hypertrophy is insufficient and patient fitness allows.  
- After completion of liver surgery, resume adjuvant systemic therapy (same regimen or adapted based on response) for at least 6 months.  
- Monitor CEA and imaging every 3 months during the first year.

- FLR ratio compatibility with surgery (future liver remnant volume).  
- Detailed hepatic segment involvement and presence/absence of vascular or biliary invasion.  
- Status of the primary colon tumor (already resected or not).  
- Whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been given and the response achieved.  
- Liver MRI results for precise lesion mapping and volumetry.

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, right T4aN2 colon cancer, ten bilobar liver metastases (1-4 cm) at the abdominal CT scan, CEA 1350 ng/mL, BRAF wild-type. Liver MRI: contact with IVC and left portal branch.
MDT Discussion: Not initially resectable, induction therapy planned before re-evaluation.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The MDT has already judged the disease “not initially resectable” because of bilobar distribution, vascular contact (IVC and left portal branch) and the high tumor burden (10 lesions, 1‑4 cm). The analysis lists a prerequisite action – “induction therapy planned before re‑evaluation” – that must be completed before a definitive surgical decision can be made. In addition, a decisive piece of missing information is the future liver remnant (FLR) ratio, which directly determines whether a safe hepatic resection is feasible. Because both a specific pre‑operative treatment and a key missing metric are identified, the case fits the “Potentially resectable” category.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- 1️⃣ Confirm that the primary right‑colon tumor has not yet been resected (Missing item). If still in situ, schedule a curative‑intent colectomy either before or concurrently with liver surgery after systemic down‑staging, provided no obstruction or perforation is present (obstruction = False, perforation = False).  
- 2️⃣ Initiate systemic chemotherapy immediately (no prior systemic treatment reported). Preferred regimen: 3‑6 months of intensive doublet or triplet therapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI) combined with an anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) because the tumor is BRAF wild‑type; RAS status should be obtained if not already known.  
- 3️⃣ Perform baseline staging of extra‑hepatic sites: obtain a thoraco‑CT scan (currently “ThoracoCTScanPerformed: False”) and consider bone scan or MRI if clinically indicated (bone involvement Missing). This will confirm the absence of pulmonary or skeletal disease.  
- 4️⃣ After 3‑4 months of chemotherapy, repeat imaging: contrast‑enhanced liver MRI and abdominal CT to reassess number, size, and vascular involvement of metastases, and to calculate the FLR ratio (currently Missing). If FLR is insufficient, plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or consider a two‑stage hepatectomy/ALPPS strategy.  
- 5️⃣ If restaging shows adequate tumor response (e.g., ≤30 % residual disease) and FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % in a cirrhotic liver), proceed to liver resection. Given bilobar disease and vascular contact, a staged approach (e.g., right‑plus‑left hepatectomy in two operations, or combined portal embolization followed by a single extended resection) is advisable. Intra‑operative ultrasound should be used to refine resection margins and assess vascular invasion.  
- 6️⃣ Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (continuation of the pre‑operative regimen) for a total of 6‑12 months, with consideration of targeted therapy based on final molecular profiling (e.g., anti‑EGFR continuation if RAS wild‑type).  
- 7️⃣ Serial CEA monitoring (baseline 1350 ng/mL) and imaging every 3‑4 months during follow‑up.

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Grade of differentiation of the primary tumor (impacts prognosis and may influence the aggressiveness of systemic therapy).  
- Confirmation of whether the primary colon cancer has already been resected.  
- Detailed hepatic segment involvement and arterial anatomy (necessary for planning the extent of hepatectomy and vascular control).  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio and volumetry (critical to decide if a safe resection is possible).  
- Results of thoraco‑CT (to exclude pulmonary metastases) and bone imaging (to exclude skeletal disease).  
- RAS mutation status (required to determine suitability of anti‑EGFR therapy).  
These missing items are the most pivotal for finalizing resectability and tailoring the therapeutic sequence.

Case_Content:
Woman, 50 years old, T3N1M1 rectal cancer, five liver metastases (segments II, III, IVa, VI, VII), max size 4.1 cm. CEA 370 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Extensive bilobar involvement, possibility of conversion depending on response to chemotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: current data are insufficient to declare the liver disease resectable upfront because (a) no cross‑sectional imaging of the chest, abdomen or liver MRI has been performed to confirm absence of extra‑hepatic disease and to delineate vascular anatomy, (b) the future liver remnant volume/FLR ratio is unknown, and (c) it is not stated whether the rectal primary has been resected or requires neoadjuvant therapy. These missing pieces are decisive for surgical feasibility; therefore resection will require systemic chemotherapy (and possibly radiotherapy) followed by restaging imaging before a definitive operative plan can be made.  

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic chemotherapy appropriate for KRAS‑mutated metastatic rectal cancer (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) with the goal of tumor downsizing and assessment of biologic response.  
- Simultaneously arrange staging investigations: contrast‑enhanced CT of chest, abdomen, pelvis and a liver‑specific MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to (i) exclude pulmonary or other extra‑hepatic metastases, (ii) define the exact size, number, vascular and biliary relationships of each hepatic lesion, and (iii) calculate the FLR volume.  
- Evaluate the rectal primary: if symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding) or if not yet resected, plan for neoadjuvant long‑course chemoradiotherapy followed by total mesorectal excision; if asymptomatic and resectable, consider upfront primary resection before liver surgery.  
- After 2–4 months of chemotherapy, repeat imaging to assess response. If sufficient tumor shrinkage and FLR ≥20‑30 % (or ≥40 % after chemotherapy‑induced liver injury) is confirmed, proceed to liver surgery.  
- Because disease is bilobar (segments II, III, IVa, VI, VII), plan a staged hepatectomy: (i) first stage – clearance of lesions in the right liver (segments VI, VII) possibly combined with portal vein embolization of the right portal branch to hypertrophy the left liver, (ii) second stage – resection of left‑lateral lesions (segments II, III, IVa) after adequate FLR hypertrophy.  
- If FLR remains inadequate after PVE, consider associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) or extensive parenchymal‑sparing resections/ablation.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy to complete a total of 6‑8 months systemic therapy, with surveillance CEA and imaging.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Status of the rectal primary (resected or not, presence of obstructive/bleeding symptoms).  
- Complete staging imaging: thoraco‑abdominal CT and liver MRI with vascular mapping.  
- Future liver remnant volume/FLR ratio and hepatic arterial/portal anatomy.  
- Presence or absence of vascular or biliary involvement of the metastases.  
- Whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been administered and the tumor’s radiologic response.  
- Confirmation of absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, nodes, bone, brain).  

These items are essential to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.

Case_Content:
Man, 62 years old, operated 4 years ago for right colon adenocarcinoma (T3N1M0), no initial recurrence. Surveillance: CEA 180 ng/mL. At the thoraco-abdominal CT scan: two liver lesions segments V and VIII, 2.8 and 3.2 cm. Liver MRI confirms no other foci. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Isolated metachronous metastases, anatomically accessible, good general condition.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Category: Resectable upfront  
Reasoning: The structured analysis shows two metachronous liver metastases (NumberOfMetastases = 2) located in segments V and VIII with maximum diameter 3.2 cm, no extra‑hepatic disease (ExtrahepaticPulmonaryInvolvement = False, ExtrahepaticPeritonealInvolvement = False, ExtrahepaticLymphNodeInvolvement = False, ExtrahepaticBoneInvolvement = False). The lesions are anatomically accessible (MDT comment: “anatomically accessible”) and the patient is in good general condition. In the absence of reported vascular or biliary invasion, a limited hepatic resection (segmentectomy or non‑anatomic wedge) is technically feasible and would leave an adequate future liver remnant in a non‑cirrhotic liver. Therefore surgery can be offered without mandatory pre‑operative down‑staging.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Proceed to curative‑intent hepatic surgery: perform parenchymal‑sparing resection of the lesions (segment V and segment VIII wedge/segmentectomy) aiming for R0 margins.  
• Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion boundaries, assess for any occult disease, and verify vascular anatomy (since “ArterialAnatomy” is missing).  
• Post‑operative pathology to document margin status, tumor grade, and confirm KRAS mutation.  
• After recovery (≈4–6 weeks), initiate adjuvant systemic therapy because the primary tumor was KRAS‑mutated (anti‑EGFR agents ineffective). Recommended regimen: 6 months of FOLFOX (or CAPOX) combined with bevacizumab, per current guidelines for resected colorectal liver metastases with high‑risk features (elevated CEA = 180 ng/mL).  
• Continue CEA surveillance and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
The most critical missing items that could modify the plan are:  
- Future Liver Remnant (FLR) ratio – needed to confirm that resection will leave ≥30 % functional liver in a normal liver.  
- Detailed vascular and biliary involvement (PresenceOfVascularContactOrInvasion, PresenceOfBiliaryStructuresInvolved, ArterialAnatomy) – essential to ensure safe resection and to plan intra‑operative management.  
- Liver function tests / underlying liver disease assessment (not listed) – to corroborate FLR adequacy.  
- Primary tumor pathology details (grade, margin status, peritoneal invasion) – useful for overall prognostication but less likely to change immediate hepatic surgery.

Woman, 70 years old, operated for low rectal cancer 3 years ago (T3N1M0) after chemoradiotherapy. CEA 95 ng/mL. Liver MRI: lesion in segment II (2.5 cm) and micronodule segment V. RAS wild-type, MSS.
MDT Discussion: Metachronous metastases, potentially curable, negative extra-hepatic workup.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning: The liver disease consists of two small metastases (2.5 cm in segment II and a micronodule in segment V) without reported vascular or biliary invasion, which would generally allow a parenchyma‑sparing resection. However, the structured analysis lists the following decisive missing items:  
- Future Liver Remnant (FLR) ratio compatibility with surgery (Missing) – needed to confirm that the remaining liver volume will be sufficient after resection.  
- Presence of vascular contact or invasion (Missing) – required to determine whether an anatomic resection or vascular reconstruction is necessary.  
- Thoraco‑CT scan (Missing) – needed to definitively exclude pulmonary metastases that would change the curative intent.  

Because these specific pieces of information are absent, the case cannot be classified as “Resectable upfront”; a prerequisite assessment (FLR calculation and complete thoracic imaging) must be completed before a definitive surgical plan can be made.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Complete staging  
   - Obtain a contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary metastases.  
   - Perform bone imaging (bone scan or MRI) if clinically indicated, given the missing data on skeletal disease.  
   - Conduct a volumetric CT or MRI of the liver to calculate the FLR ratio and assess arterial/portal anatomy.  

2. Systemic therapy (neoadjuvant)  
   - Initiate 3 months of peri‑operative chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX ± bevacizumab).  
   - Because the tumor is RAS‑wild‑type and left‑sided, consider adding an anti‑EGFR agent (cetuximab or panitumumab) if the multidisciplinary team deems it appropriate and the patient tolerates it.  
   - Monitor CEA trend and radiologic response; a decrease in CEA and stable or regressive lesions will support proceeding to surgery.  

3. Re‑assessment after chemotherapy  
   - Repeat liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to evaluate lesion size, vascular involvement, and to repeat FLR calculation.  
   - If FLR ≥ 20 % (or ≥30 % in a steatotic liver) and no vascular invasion is identified, plan curative liver resection.  

4. Surgical plan (contingent on adequate FLR)  
   - Perform a segmentectomy of segment II (2.5 cm lesion) and a limited wedge or non‑anatomic resection of the segment V micronodule, preserving maximal parenchyma.  
   - If FLR is insufficient, schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) of the right liver to induce hypertrophy, then repeat FLR assessment before resection.  

5. Post‑operative management  
   - Complete adjuvant systemic therapy to reach a total of 6 months (or longer per MDT recommendation) after surgery.  
   - Serial CEA monitoring and imaging surveillance every 3–6 months for the first 2 years.

- Future Liver Remnant (FLR) ratio – essential to confirm that the patient can tolerate the planned hepatic resection.  
- Presence of vascular contact/invasion – determines whether a simple parenchyma‑sparing resection is feasible or if more extensive vascular control is required.  
- Thoraco‑CT (or PET‑CT) results – needed to definitively exclude pulmonary metastases, which would alter the curative intent.  
- Bone imaging (if clinically indicated) – to rule out skeletal disease that is currently listed as Missing.  

These missing items must be obtained before finalizing the surgical approach.

- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy should be continued to complete a total of 6 months of systemic therapy, adjusting regimen based on response and tolerability.  
- Throughout, maintain multidisciplinary surveillance with serial CEA and imaging every 3–4 months.

- Detailed vascular and biliary anatomy of the lesions (presence of portal/hepatic vein contact or invasion).  
- Confirmation that a thoraco‑abdominal CT has been performed to rule out occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
- Status of any prior systemic therapy or liver‑directed treatment.

Case_Content:
Woman, 63 years old, rectal tumor operated 3 years earlier (T3N1M0). Surveillance liver MRI: segment VIII lesion, 2.8 cm, hypermetabolic on PET. No other foci on PET. KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Single metachronous metastasis, accessible, good general condition.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
• Classification: Resectable upfront  
• Reasoning: The structured analysis shows a solitary 2.8 cm metastasis confined to segment VIII, described as “accessible” with no PET‑positive extra‑hepatic disease. The patient is in good general condition, and a single peripheral lesion of this size is routinely amenable to an anatomic segmentectomy or non‑anatomic wedge resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant in a non‑cirrhotic liver. No contraindicating vascular, biliary or infiltrative features are reported, and there is no evidence of extra‑hepatic spread.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Confirm staging – Obtain a contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT if not already done) to definitively exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease and to assess arterial/portal anatomy and liver volumetry (FLR).  
2. Proceed to liver surgery – Perform a laparoscopic or open segment VIII resection (segmentectomy or wedge) ensuring negative margins (R0). Intra‑operative ultrasound should be used to verify lesion location and to assess any unsuspected vascular contact.  
3. Pathology review – After resection, obtain detailed pathology including margin status, tumor grade, and KRAS status (already known) to guide adjuvant therapy.  
4. Adjuvant systemic therapy – Because the primary tumor was KRAS‑mutated and the metastasis is metachronous, prescribe 6 months of adjuvant chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPOX) following recovery from surgery, per current NCCN/EUROCARE guidelines for resected colorectal liver metastasis.  
5. Surveillance – Schedule CEA monitoring every 3 months for the first 2 years, and imaging (contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI) every 6 months, adjusting based on pathology risk factors (margin status, grade, etc.).  

Step 3 – Missing data  
• Future Liver Remnant (FLR) ratio – Needed to confirm that the planned resection will leave sufficient functional liver volume; if FLR <20 % (normal liver) a portal vein embolization or alternative strategy would be required.  
• Vascular and biliary involvement – Confirmation that the lesion does not abut major hepatic veins, portal branches, or biliary ducts is essential for safe resection.  
• Comprehensive thoraco‑abdominal CT – To definitively rule out occult extra‑hepatic metastases and to provide detailed anatomy for surgical planning.  
• Primary tumor pathology details (grade, margin status, peritoneal invasion, emboli) – Important for overall prognostication and may influence the intensity or duration of adjuvant therapy.  
These missing items are the most critical to validate the “Resectable upfront” decision and to fine‑tune the peri‑operative plan.

Category: Potentially resectable

Moreover, given the markedly elevated CEA (380 ng/mL) and high‑risk primary (T4 N2), neoadjuvant systemic chemotherapy is advisable to assess tumor biology before committing to major hepatic resection. Because a specific prerequisite (systemic chemotherapy and definitive FLR assessment) is needed, the case fits the “Potentially resectable” category rather than “Resectable upfront.”  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Initiate systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6 cycles of FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) to treat occult micrometastatic disease, obtain a biologic response assessment, and potentially downsize the liver lesions.  
2. After chemotherapy, repeat high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast and a volumetric CT to:  
   – Determine the exact segmental distribution of the four lesions (bilobar).  
   – Measure the FLR ratio; if FLR < 30 % (normal liver) or < 40 % (post‑chemotherapy liver), plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy.  
   – Assess for vascular or biliary involvement that would dictate the need for complex reconstructions.  
3. If FLR is adequate and no major vascular invasion is identified, proceed to a single‑stage, parenchyma‑sparing liver resection (e.g., right hepatectomy with left‑lateral wedge resections) using intra‑operative ultrasound to guide margins.  
4. If FLR is insufficient or lesions are widely separated, employ a staged approach:  
   – Stage 1: PVE of the liver portion to be resected (or ALPPS if rapid hypertrophy is required).  
   – Re‑image after 2–4 weeks; if FLR has hypertrophied to safe limits, perform Stage 2 – definitive liver resection.  
5. Post‑operative: resume adjuvant chemotherapy to complete a total of 12 months of systemic therapy, given the high‑risk primary pathology and elevated CEA.  
6. Surveillance: CEA every 3 months and cross‑sectional imaging (MRI or CT) every 6 months for the first 2 years.

- FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery (future liver remnant volume).  
- HepaticSegmentsInvolved (precise location of each metastasis).  
- PresenceOfVascularContactOrInvasion (relationship to hepatic veins, portal pedicle, hepatic artery).  
- PresenceOfBiliaryStructuresInvolved (risk of biliary reconstruction).  
- GradeOfDifferentiation of the primary tumor (prognostic impact).  
- PreviousResectionMargins and PeritonealInvasion status (risk of residual disease).  
- Confirmation that no systemic chemotherapy has already been delivered (to schedule neoadjuvant therapy appropriately).  
These items must be clarified before finalizing the surgical plan.

• Perform high-resolution contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships and to calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Given the high CEA level (240 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to confirm absence of additional occult lesions.

B. Consider short peri-operative systemic therapy
• Given the elevated CEA level (240 ng/mL) and relatively early recurrence (2 years), a short course (2–3 months) of peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) is advisable to treat micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology.
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.

C. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT-scan after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and reassess lesion relationships.

D. Surgical management after restaging
• If resectability is confirmed, perform parenchymal-sparing wedge/segmental resections or ablation of segments II and VIII guided by intra-operative ultrasound.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of both lesions on MRI.
B. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy 
D. Details of any adjuvant chemotherapy received after the initial rectal surgery.
F. Exact CEA trend over time prior to detection of the lesions.
G. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 58 years old, left T4aN2M1 colon cancer with multiple bilobar metastases. After 6 cycles FOLFOX + bevacizumab: 60% volumetric reduction, CEA dropped from 880 to 180 ng/mL. Liver MRI: 5 remaining lesions, well-defined.
MDT Discussion: Major response to chemotherapy, surgical conversion considered.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning: The patient shows a major radiologic and biochemical response to systemic therapy (60 % volumetric reduction, CEA ↓ from 880 to 180 ng/mL) and now has five well‑defined liver lesions, suggesting that surgical conversion may be feasible. However, decisive information required to confirm technical and oncologic feasibility is missing: the exact size and segmental distribution of each lesion, presence of vascular or biliary involvement, the future liver remnant (FLR) ratio, and the status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not, presence of obstructive/bleeding symptoms). Moreover, the absence of documented extra‑hepatic staging (chest CT, peritoneal, nodal, bone, brain) precludes a definitive “resectable upfront” classification. Therefore the case is deemed potentially resectable pending completion of these assessments.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Complete systemic therapy: administer additional cycles of FOLFOX + bevacizumab to reach a total of 12 cycles (or until maximal response), unless toxicity dictates earlier transition.  
2. Restaging work‑up:  
   • Perform contrast‑enhanced CT of chest, abdomen, pelvis (or PET‑CT) to rule out occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
   • Obtain high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast and 3‑D volumetry to define lesion size, segmental involvement, vascular/biliary contact, and calculate FLR.  
   • Re‑measure CEA and obtain baseline tumor markers.  
3. Evaluate primary tumor:  
   • If the left‑sided primary has not been resected, schedule colon resection (segmental colectomy) either before or simultaneously with liver surgery, provided no obstruction, perforation, or bleeding is present.  
   • Obtain molecular profiling (RAS, BRAF, MSI) on the primary specimen to guide adjuvant systemic choices.  
4. Surgical planning based on liver findings:  
   • If FLR ≥ 30 % (≥ 40 % in steatotic liver) and lesions are amenable to parenchymal‑sparing resections, plan a single‑stage, margin‑negative (R0) hepatectomy using anatomic or non‑anatomic resections.  
   • If FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or a staged hepatectomy (two‑stage or ALPPS) to hypertrophy the remnant.  
   • Aim for ≤ 4 cm margin where possible; use intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion clearance.  
5. Post‑operative management:  
   • Resume systemic therapy (e.g., continuation of bevacizumab‑containing regimen or switch to a different biologic based on molecular profile) for 3–6 months as adjuvant treatment.  
   • Monitor CEA and imaging every 3–4 months for recurrence.  

Step 3 – Missing data (most crucial for final decision)  
• Status of the colorectal primary tumor (resected vs. unresected, presence of obstruction, perforation, or bleeding).  
• Molecular phenotype of the primary (RAS, BRAF, MSI status).  
• Detailed hepatic lesion characteristics: maximum/minimum diameter, exact hepatic segments involved, proximity to major vessels or bile ducts, presence of vascular/biliary invasion.  
• Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio and volumetric assessment.  
• Comprehensive extra‑hepatic staging: chest CT (pulmonary mets), abdominal/pelvic CT or MRI for peritoneal, nodal, bone, and brain involvement.  
• Arterial anatomy and any atypical features that could affect resection strategy.  

These items must be obtained before a definitive surgical plan can be finalized.

Case_Content:
Man, 65 years old, sigmoid tumor with eight bilobar liver metastases. After 4 months FOLFIRI: radiological stability, CEA unchanged at 420 ng/mL. Thoracic CT scan negative for metastases.
MDT Discussion: Stable disease, not resectable, discussion on continuing systemic therapy.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: current data indicate 8 bilobar liver metastases with radiological stability after 4 months of FOLFIRI, but critical information required to determine surgical feasibility is missing. Specifically, (a) the primary sigmoid tumor has not been confirmed as resected, and (b) detailed hepatic imaging (contrast‑enhanced abdomen CT or liver MRI) and volumetric assessment (future liver remnant ratio) are absent, preventing an accurate evaluation of lesion size, vascular/biliary involvement, and functional liver reserve. These prerequisites must be addressed before a definitive resection plan can be made.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Continue systemic therapy while obtaining molecular profiling of the primary tumor (RAS, BRAF, MSI status) to guide targeted or immunologic agents.  
- Arrange high‑quality liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast (or multiphase CT) and CT volumetry to define lesion dimensions, vascular contact, and calculate FLR.  
- Evaluate the need for primary tumor control: if symptomatic or to prevent future complications, schedule sigmoid resection (open or laparoscopic) now; if asymptomatic, primary resection can be coordinated with liver surgery after conversion therapy.  
- Pursue conversion chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFIRI + anti‑VEGF or switch to FOLFOX + targeted agent) aiming for tumor shrinkage to allow a curative‑intent liver resection (potentially a two‑stage hepatectomy or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy, ALPPS, depending on future liver remnant).  
- Re‑assess resectability after 2–3 months of additional systemic therapy using the newly obtained imaging and FLR data.  
- If sufficient down‑staging is achieved, plan either simultaneous resection of primary and liver metastases (if FLR adequate) or staged approach (primary first, then liver).  
- If conversion fails, consider liver‑directed therapies (e.g., hepatic arterial infusion, radio‑embolization) or continue systemic therapy as palliative intent.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Confirmation of whether the sigmoid primary has already been resected.  
- Detailed hepatic imaging (contrast‑enhanced abdomen CT or liver MRI) to define lesion size, vascular/biliary involvement, and arterial anatomy.  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio and volumetric compatibility with surgery.  
- Histopathologic grade of differentiation and molecular phenotype (RAS/BRAF/MSI) of the primary tumor.  
- Presence or absence of symptoms from the primary tumor (obstruction, bleeding, perforation).  
- Assessment of possible extra‑hepatic peritoneal or bone disease (currently missing).  

These items are essential to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.
